# Preface {.unnumbered}

This is the student-facing book for a four-week, pass/fail elective on AI in
medicine for fourth-year medical students. Its one idea: **it is your job to
learn where AI helps your work, and you learn that by trying.** The chapters
are a guide, not assignments. They give you a framework; they do not try to
teach everything. Each week has one core chapter and a menu to choose from,
and most of your learning happens when you [use AI to teach
yourself](course/learn-with-ai.qmd). Each chapter stands alone. Nothing in the
book needs an install, a paid account, or a real patient.

## How to read a chapter

Read what helps you with the week's work, and skip what does not. Every
chapter has the same parts, in the same order:

1. **In short.** A box at the top: the main idea, what you do, what you keep,
   and which sections to read if you are short on time. The subtitle under
   the chapter title gives the honest total time.
2. **What you'll learn, and what you need.** The objectives, the course
   competencies the chapter serves, and what you need for the activity.
   Usually that is only your university account.
3. **An opening scenario.** A clinical situation you will recognize, before
   any jargon.
4. **Why this matters.** What changes for you in residency, which starts
   next July.
5. **How it works.** The idea, in prose, with figures and tables.
6. **Watch or listen.** One video or podcast episode, with a note on what to
   listen for and where you can stop.
7. **Do.** The activity, written so you can finish it alone. It starts with a
   task that works, and it ends with something you keep. Wherever it touches
   the literature, you choose your specialty.
8. **Check.** A rubric you score yourself against.
9. **What this changes for you.** The standing question, *what does this
   change about how you'll practice?* The scenario from the opening comes back
   with a better answer.
10. **Go deeper.** Papers, talks, and videos. Claims nobody has yet checked
    are flagged `[VERIFY]` and left flagged until someone has.

There is no summary at the bottom; the "In short" box at the top does that
job. The competencies are named by code, `AIM-1` through `AIM-9` and `AIM-X`;
the coverage table below says what each one is.

The safety rules are short. **Use your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot
account. Never put real patient information into a course activity. Check what
matters before you rely on it. You sign the note.**

Four ideas recur across the chapters, and each is named the same way wherever
it appears. **Proxies fail**: almost every AI failure in medicine is a stand-in
that looked reasonable. **Efficiency gains get eaten by volume**: per-unit
savings are cancelled out by growth in use. **The published number is the
optimistic one**: the most prominently reported statistic is nearly always the
best case. **Who benefits, who bears the risk, who decides**: the people a
tool helps are often not the people it puts at risk, or the people who chose
it. A chapter that uses one of these says so.

## The chapters, week by week

Each week has one **core** chapter, which goes with Monday's talk, and a
**menu** to choose from by interest. The [syllabus](course/syllabus.qmd) gives
the live sessions, the weekly routine, and the due dates. Each week you also write a short
[learning journal](course/learning-journal.qmd) entry about what you tried.
Whoever runs the course reads the [For instructors](appendix/instructors.qmd)
appendix.

**Week 1, working with AI**

- Thursday's hands-on session: [Plan your four weeks with
  ChatGPT](chapters/plan-your-learning.qmd): research what the field expects,
  then build your own plan.
- Core: [How these systems work](chapters/core-foundations.qmd): the eGFR is a
  model you already trust, and the chatbot is the same loop with words.

**Week 2, getting good at it**

- Core: [Prompting lab](chapters/enrichment-prompting-lab.qmd): getting good
  answers, and knowing their limits.
- Menu: [Critical appraisal](chapters/core-appraisal.qmd),
  [Bias and equity](chapters/core-bias-equity.qmd),
  [Grounding AI in real sources](chapters/enrichment-rag-notebooklm.qmd),
  [Writing with AI and still sounding like you](chapters/enrichment-writing-voice.qmd).

**Week 3, AI and your patients**

- Core: [Talking to patients about AI](chapters/core-patient-communication.qmd).
- Menu: [Agentic coding](chapters/enrichment-agentic-coding.qmd): build a
  clinical tool in an hour, then test it; the
  [scribe open lab](appendix/open-labs.qmd).

**Week 4, responsibility**

- Core: [Ethics: what you owe when you sign the note](chapters/core-ethics-regulation.qmd).
- Menu: [Will AI take your job?](chapters/enrichment-workforce-economics.qmd),
  [What AI costs the planet](chapters/enrichment-environment.qmd).

## Competency coverage

The course tags every chapter to a stable competency ID so it can be mapped
to national standards when they arrive. Where the IDs come from, and the
frameworks behind them, is in the appendix [What the field
expects](appendix/competency-frameworks.qmd); the coverage rules are in
`curriculum/competencies.md` in the repository. In short: AIM-1 foundations;
AIM-2 critical appraisal; AIM-3 bias and equity; AIM-4 ethics, law, and
regulation; AIM-5 clinical use; AIM-6 talking to patients; AIM-7 workflow and
systems; AIM-8 health data science; AIM-9 research and scholarship; AIM-X
professional identity, the closing question.

The four core chapters make AIM-2, AIM-4, AIM-5, and AIM-6 main subjects, and
the week 1 live talks cover AIM-1. AIM-3, bias and equity, is not in a core
chapter: it is covered by the bias chapter on the menu. That is a deliberate choice for this offering, made so the core
can focus on using AI well. AIM-8, health data science, is not the main subject
of any chapter; the foundations chapter covers training and test sets, area
under the curve, and dataset shift along the way. Every Check is scored by you
against a rubric, so "practised" here means self-assessed, not graded.

## How this book was made

This book was built with AI: AI agents drafted most of the text under the
author's direction, and the author decides what is published. The appendix
[How this book was made](appendix/about.qmd) and the [AI
ledger](appendix/ai-ledger.qmd) say what the AI did and what a person checked,
because the course asks you to disclose and verify, and the book does the same.
